title: Cognitive Load Theory: Emerging Trends and Innovations
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick annotates ten papers from a new special issue on Cognitive Load Theory, pairing each summary with a 'What do teachers need to know?' judgement. His framing is that CLT has moved beyond its lab origins and is now testing how motivation, interest, emotion, self-regulation and immersive technology interact with cognitive load. Across the notes he draws out classroom implications: students can be taught to self-manage split-attention materials; interleaving works through discrimination learning rather than spacing, a distinction he warns could become a lethal mutation; worked examples mainly helped students with a mastery orientation; and reading slides aloud creates harmful verbal redundancy. He treats interest as a corrective to engagement-first thinking, since it raises effort only on tasks within reach, and argues that mixed reality does not substitute for sound instructional design. The piece is a critical digest rather than an original argument, but its consistent move is to test each finding against what teachers would actually change.
points: Hendrick's warning on interleaving is the sharpest point: its benefit comes from discriminating between similar-looking problem types, not from spacing, so spacing practice for its own sake misses the mechanism.
The redundancy study leads to a concrete slide rule - pair spoken explanation with visuals, not with the same words on screen - while noting it did not reproduce the classic modality effect.
He reads the interest-and-effort paper as evidence that for hard content, clear explanation, scaffolding and sequencing matter more than making material exciting.
The worked-example study complicates a well-evidenced effect: gains were concentrated among students with a mastery goal orientation, and prior knowledge alone predicted transfer.
On mixed reality and animations he stresses that technology changes perceived effort more than outcomes, and that transient information must be chunked with pauses.
quotes: Since its inception in the 1980s, Cognitive Load Theory has informed our understanding of how learning happens and instructional design by systematically explaining how the architecture of human cognition constrains learning. For many educators it’s been a very useful theoretical lens through which to think about designing lessons and helping students learn new concepts but it has also been disputed in some quarters, specifically how we measure cognitive load.

If you teach in resource-constrained settings, this is empowering: a few minutes spent modelling how to annotate and mentally “connect the dots” could make a real difference in how students handle complex material. The study doesn’t claim big gains either but reducing mental strain for the same result is a win, especially for struggling learners.

When they interleaved math and language topics (which created spacing between similar content), they found no learning advantage over blocked practice. This suggests that the benefits of interleaving come specifically from discrimination learning, ie helping students learn to distinguish between similar problem types rather than from the spacing effect.

This paper is particularly relevant in an era of over-produced slides and multimedia lessons. It shows that adding more modes of input like reading slides out loud while students are also reading them, can backfire.

This is a helpful corrective to the idea that “engagement” solves everything. Yes, students who are interested in a topic are more likely to put in the effort, but only when the material is within reach. When things get tough, interest alone isn’t enough.

This study is a helpful reminder that flashy technology doesn't replace sound instructional design. If you’re using VR or AR in the classroom, the key is to make sure the instructions are spatially aligned with the visuals, just like you would on a worksheet or PowerPoint slide.

I guess the next frontier will inevitably be how AI informs the field, but this special issue shows that CLT has much to offer any area where human learning is considered in detail. What stands out across these papers is not just the consistency of core principles like split attention and redundancy, but how researchers are starting to test those ideas in more complex, realistic, and tech-rich learning environments.
